To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the conventional measure of decentralisation is not a good proxy for the degree of fiscal autonomy of subnational governments; (2) revenue autonomy and expenditure autonomy are two distinct concepts, and (3) both revenue autonomy and expenditure decentralisation are important determinants of the quality of fiscal decentralisation, but they are not substitutes for each other.

(1) the conventional measure of fiscal decentralisation (the subnational share in total government expenditures) is a very poor indicator for the extent of revenue autonomy, and that (2) the conventional measure is also a poor indicator of the degree of fiscal dependence on the federal government, which is measured instead by the subnational share in the total amount of external grants.

(i) the conventional decentralisation indicators are not sufficient for capturing the extent of decentralisation, (ii) they are not sufficient for studying the effects of decentralisation, and (iii) the effects of decentralization are heterogeneous.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing an empirically useful taxonomy of decentralisation indicators and with the implications of such a taxonomy for the analysis of fiscal decentralisation.
the measurement of decentralisation.
how to measure the extent of fiscal and administrative decentralisation, and the relationship among these measures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

decentralisation is a multidimensional phenomenon that cannot be captured by any single indicator, but that the different dimensions should enter regression analyses in the most flexible way possible.
the extent of decentralisation is a multidimensional phenomenon, and that the choice of the appropriate decentralisation measure should be based on the research question.
decentralisation is a multidimensional concept and that each aspect of it should be considered separately.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
decentralisation measures should be used with caution, and that their use should be informed by their theoretical and empirical underpinnings.
decentralisation is a complex phenomenon, which can be decomposed into distinct components that should be treated as such in empirical work.
decentralisation should be measured in a multidimensional way and that the distinct dimensions should be allowed to enter the regression analysis separately.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single measure of decentralisation cannot be used to explain all outcomes of interest.

the conventional decentralisation measures are only proxies to the underlying decentralisation process and that their explanatory power depends on how well the proxy captures the true underlying decentralisation process.
a more careful consideration of the different aspects of fiscal decentralisation and their interrelations is needed in empirical studies.
